steps.tx: Spinal cord hemisection produces a distinctive pattern of dissociated sensory and motor loss. **Brown-Séquard** syndrome is characterized by ipsilateral spastic paresis below the lesion due to disruption of the descending **corticospinal** tract, alongside ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration sensation from dorsal column interruption. Concurrently, it produces contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation beginning 1 to 2 dermatomal segments below the level of the lesion.
steps.say: Brown Séquard syndrome arises from hemisection of the spinal cord, most commonly caused by penetrating trauma or lateral disc herniation. Disruption of descending corticospinal tracts produces ipsilateral spastic paralysis below the lesion. Interruption of the dorsal columns causes ipsilateral loss of vibration and joint position sense, while spinothalamic disruption causes contralateral loss of pain and temperature.

steps.tx: Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery results in extensive spinal cord infarction. **Anterior spinal artery** syndrome causes acute bilateral flaccid paraplegia below the lesion and loss of pain and temperature sensation. Because the dorsal third of the spinal cord is supplied separately by paired posterior spinal arteries, there is complete preservation of **posterior column** vibration and joint position sensation. Sphincter paralysis with acute urinary retention is an invariable accompanying feature.
steps.say: Anterior spinal artery syndrome produces acute infarction of the anterior two thirds of the spinal cord. Patients develop sudden bilateral flaccid paralysis and loss of pain and temperature sensations below the level of the infarct. Crucially, posterior column modalities including vibration and proprioception remain entirely intact because posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns.

points: Bilateral motor paralysis below the level of the lesion

right.title: Posterior Cord Syndrome
points: Isolated loss of vibration and proprioceptive sensation

steps.tx: Incomplete cervical cord contusion produces disproportionate neurological deficits. **Central cord syndrome** occurs characteristically following cervical **hyperextension** injuries in older individuals with preexisting cervical spondylotic canal stenosis. The central cord contusion preferentially damages the medially situated cervical motor fibers of the corticospinal tracts, producing marked motor weakness in the upper extremities with relative preservation of lower extremity strength.
steps.say: Central cord syndrome represents the most common incomplete spinal cord injury, typically occurring after cervical hyperextension trauma in elderly patients with cervical canal stenosis. Compression damages the medially located cervical motor fibers of the corticospinal tract, producing disproportionately severe motor weakness in the arms compared to the legs.

rows: Hyperextension in a stenotic cervical canal

steps.tx: Cystic cavitation of the central spinal cord generates a pathognomonic sensory deficit pattern. **Syringomyelia** involves progressive longitudinal cavitation (syrinx) within the periependymal gray matter of the spinal cord. Expanding fluid cavities disrupt the decussating fibers of the lateral spinothalamic tract, producing a suspended cape-like distribution of **dissociated sensory loss** characterized by loss of pain and temperature sensation with preserved light touch and vibration across the shoulders and arms.
steps.say: Syringomyelia is characterized by a fluid filled cavity within the central spinal cord that expands to disrupt the crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure. This produces a suspended cape like distribution of dissociated sensory loss across the shoulders and arms, characterized by loss of pain and temperature sensations with intact light touch and vibration.

steps.tx: Structural hindbrain herniation is intimately linked to the pathogenesis of cervical syringomyelia. **Chiari** type 1 malformation features caudal herniation of peg-like cerebellar tonsils greater than 5 mm below the **foramen magnum**. Disrupted pulsatile cerebrospinal fluid dynamics at the craniovertebral junction drives fluid dissection into the spinal cord parenchyma, generating cervical syringomyelia in over 50% of symptomatic patients. Suboccipital craniectomy and foramen magnum decompression restore CSF flow.
steps.say: Chiari type one malformation is defined by downward herniation of cerebellar tonsils more than five millimeters below the foramen magnum. Impeded cerebrospinal fluid flow at the craniocervical junction causes chronic pulsatile dissection into the spinal cord, causing syringomyelia in over half of symptomatic patients. Posterior fossa bony decompression provides normal cerebrospinal fluid dynamics.

steps.tx: Compressive lesions of the distal spinal cord require urgent localization. **Conus medullaris** syndrome localizes to the L1-L2 vertebral level, terminating the spinal cord. It presents with sudden, early, symmetrical perianal sensory loss termed **saddle anesthesia**, early urinary and fecal incontinence, bilateral symmetrical leg weakness, and absent Achilles reflexes with preserved patellar reflexes. Symmetrical onset and prominent early sphincter failure characterize conus lesions.
steps.say: Conus medullaris syndrome results from lesions at the L1-L2 vertebral level affecting the terminal sacral cord segments. Clinical features develop rapidly and symmetrically, characterized by early saddle anesthesia, early bilateral bowel and bladder incontinence, and symmetrical lower limb weakness. Early sphincter dysfunction is the hallmark of conus medullaris compression.

left.title: Conus Medullaris Syndrome
points: Lesion level at L1-L2 vertebral termination
Early, severe urinary and fecal incontinence

right.title: Cauda Equina Syndrome
points: Lesion level below L2 involving lumbosacral roots
Asymmetrical radicular leg pain and sensory loss
Late sphincter disturbance, asymmetric flaccid weakness

steps.tx: Lumbosacral nerve root compression produces distinct peripheral manifestations. **Cauda equina** syndrome arises from compression of multiple lumbosacral nerve roots below the conus medullaris. It manifests with severe, asymmetrical **radicular pain** radiating down the legs, asymmetrical flaccid lower motor neuron paraparesis, patchy asymmetric dermatomal sensory deficits, and diminished or absent lower extremity reflexes. Sphincter dysfunction occurs later in the disease course compared to conus medullaris compression.
steps.say: Cauda equina syndrome results from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots below the termination of the spinal cord. Patients characteristically present with severe asymmetrical radicular pain, patchy lower extremity weakness, and variable reflex depression. Sphincter dysfunction generally emerges later compared to conus medullaris compression.

steps.tx: Malignant epidural spinal cord compression constitutes an acute neuro-oncological emergency. Management mandates immediate administration of high-dose intravenous **dexamethasone** using a 10 to 16 mg bolus followed by 4 mg every 6 hours to reduce vasogenic cord edema. Emergency magnetic resonance imaging spanning the entire **neuraxis** must be acquired within 24 hours to detect multiple occult spinal metastases prior to emergency surgical decompression or urgent radiotherapy.
steps.say: Malignant epidural spinal cord compression demands immediate pharmacological and neuroimaging intervention. Clinicians must administer an immediate high dose intravenous dexamethasone bolus of ten to sixteen milligrams to mitigate vasogenic cord edema. Urgent magnetic resonance imaging covering the entire neuraxis must be obtained within twenty four hours to guide emergency surgical or radiation therapy.
